title: Blending the Rivers, Loosing the Flavor: Shaku Sōen’s Ambiguous Stance on Sri Lankan Buddhism and Colonialism
abstract: This articles examines the response of the Japanese Zen master Shaku Sōen 釈宗演 (1860–1919) to his experience of British colonialism on Sri Lanka from the point of view of a global history of religions. title: "Tout est dans tout:" orientalism's transformation(s) in Eugène Fromentin's Une année dans le Sahel
abstract: Inspired by the Romantic painter Delacroix and informed by the Realist literary movement, Eugène Fromentin seemingly epitomized the role of Orientalist writer-painter in the salons of Paris, where his works were read as ethnographic testimonials of life in Algeria, the newest French colony. abstract: Abstract Influenced by Natural Horsemanship ( NH ), the Japan Racing Association frames biting as a behavioral issue rooted in instinct, correctable through training. abstract: ABSTRACT “The normal exception” has long been a slogan of microhistory. abstract: 従来の日タイ関係史研究において、タイに所蔵される日本関連の写真史料は、文書史料を視覚的に補完する「挿絵」的位置づけにとどまり、一次史料として十分に活用されてこなかった。しかし写真史料は、衣装や空間配置、身体表現など、文書では詳述されない視覚的要素を提供する貴重な資料である。 そこで本研究ノートは、タイ国立公文書館「ワチラヤーン図書館と個人コレクション」棚に所蔵されるラーマ五世王・六世王期（1868～1925年）の日本関連写真に焦点をあてた。特に引出し番号18「個人（外国人）」と19「写真家」の目録カードを整理し、日本関連写真の全体像を明らかにした。 分析の結果、「個人（外国人）」には95名の外国人に関する写真情報があり、そのうち日本人は政尾藤吉、稲垣満次郎、細谷善助の3名のみであった。また「写真家」にはラーマ五世・六世王期の写真が105枚あり、そのうち細谷善助アルバム内の写真が96枚と約9割を占めていた。 …

title: ある日本人ジャーナリストの眼に映った近代中国 : 一九一〇～一九三〇年代の神田正雄を中心に
abstract: 本論文はかつて朝日新聞社に所属した中国専門の記者であった神田正雄を取り上げ、1910～1930年代におけるその活動と対中認識を論ずるものである。神田は記事、評論及び著書を通して、近代の日中関係に深く関わったほか、嶺南区域に特別な関心を持ち、世論に大きな影響を与えた人物の一人であった。 本論文では、主に四つの部分に分けて論じる。まずは、拠り所となる基本資料を紹介しながら、近代中国における神田を代表とする日本人ジャーナリストの活動状況を考察した。次に、早稲田大学在学中の中国人留学生との関わりを探り、神田の中国への関与の端緒を解明する。特に、日本人教育顧問兼教習として赴任した、四川省重慶府永川の達用学堂での活躍は高く評価されている。その上で、朝日新聞の北京特派員として対華二十一か条要求をスクープしたことに焦点を当て、1910年代における日中外交の折衝過程を描きながら、「国策」と「民意」とのはざまに置かれた神田の「真意」を探るべく考察した。最後に、視線を嶺南区域に移し、民国時期「西南派」の本拠地に注目して、神田のこの区域に対する関心の高さの理由を解明しつつ、その時の中央政府と地方勢力間の軋轢を日本に有利に動くように工夫する姿勢を検証する。かつて中国の独立や発展を真剣に考えていたであろう神田も時代とともに考えも変化し、戦時のナショナリズムの波から逃れることはできなかった。

abstract: Abstract This piece studies one of the most well-known events in the North Korean state historical narrative: the Battle of Pochonbo. title: Memory Studies and History: trajectories of an academic relationship
abstract: Against the background of how interdisciplinary Memory Studies emancipated itself from academic History over the last century, we examine current research trends through a quantitative and qualitative analysis of the two main journals of the field, namely Memory Studies and History and Memory. title: A commoning framework for environmental archaeology: beyond resource management in Indigenous North America
abstract: Environmental archaeology has often relied on common-pool resource models to interpret past human-environment relationships, yet these frameworks overlook Indigenous ontologies grounded in kinship with land, water, and more-than human beings. We propose commoning as a complementary approach that centers reciprocity, relational care, and cultural meaning alongside institutional regulation. Drawing on archaeological evidence from Virginia's Chesapeake Bay, we show how commoning reveals Indigenous environmental governance as a world-making practice. This framework advances environmental …

title: Medical Practitioners, The Archive, and the Making of Slavery in Early Modern Barbados
abstract: Abstract In seventeenth-century Barbados medical practitioners abounded, frequently operated as planters and merchants, and amassed sizeable estates. Their wills and property deeds attest to the efficacy of their professional ambitions and their important role in the formation of colonial Barbadian society. They also testify, unambiguously, to the frequency with which medical practitioners owned enslaved individuals, whose names were as prominent and more numerous in medical wills than were the names of wives, children, siblings, and friends. How should we consider this question of …

title: “Fattening” One Health: An Interspecies Approach to Dismantling the “Obesity Epidemic”
abstract: Abstract The past 30 years have been marked by the alleged public health threat of the human “obesity epidemic” and recently parallel concerns have surfaced regarding “obesity” in companion animals. Simultaneously, new research has questioned not only rising “obesity” rates but also weight as a reliable determinant of human health and it is becoming apparent that the medicalization and stigmatization of fatness have a profound effect on patients’ quality of medical care. Moreover, fat studies scholars have offered a critical perspective on how fatphobia is institutionalized within our medical …

title: From holy prince to legal ancestor: Shōtoku in Japan’s modern constitutional imagination
abstract: This article examines one strand in the modern development of the image of Prince Shōtoku (Shōtoku Taishi, 574–622), the semi-mythical statesman portrayed in the Nihon shoki as an ideal ‘sagely king’. While Shōtoku-related lore has been repeatedly reimagined, the twentieth century saw a decisive shift to a secularized image that presented him as a lay Buddhist exemplar, pioneer of diplomacy, champion of meritocracy, and architect of constitutional governance. Focusing on this last dimension, this article begins with recent examples from politics, education, and popular media that depict …

title: The Rohingya and Arakan
abstract: Abstract Using this forum's political economy and political ecology framework, this lead article reexamines the process of identifying the Rohingya as “foreign” to Arakan as one rooted in the region's uneven development. Conflicts that the British colonial state conceptualized as primarily “communal”—such as, in this case, the conflict between Rakhines, Rohingya, and Indians in Arakan—more accurately reflected a struggle to capture land and resources on the margins of empire, where economic planning was particularly privatized and uneven. This article argues that British colonial policies in …

title: Bringing the revolution home: Murayama Tomoyoshi, leftist theater, and the Chinese proletariat
abstract: This article examines how Murayama Tomoyoshi’s proletarian theater engaged with the socialist revolutionary movement in Republican China (1912–1949) to articulate proletarian solidarity between the Chinese and Japanese working-class and critique Japanese imperialism. Focusing on his two plays set in China, Account of a Violent Gang (1929) and Record of Victory (1931), I argue that Murayama conceptualized the Chinese proletariat not only as dramatic subjects but as mirrors through which Japanese audiences could recognize their own class struggles. Drawing on interviews, translated Chinese …

title: Free ports, political economy, and early globalization: Evidence from 1750s Hamburg
abstract: Abstract Recent scholarship locates the origins of modern free trade policies in the early modern free port movement. This historiography has focused on the intellectual and political history of free ports and emphasized the importance of local and regional factors in shaping trade liberalizations in different European countries and colonies. Based on evidence from eighteenth-century Hamburg, this article proposes a different reading: it argues that free trade policies emerged in response to Atlantic trade expansion. The sources suggest that merchants and magistrates were aware of the …

title: Luther Goes East: Buddhism and the Protestant Reformation in 1880s Japan
abstract: This article examines how, in the late nineteenth century, Japanese Buddhists reinterpreted the European Reformation and repurposed it as a tool for their own renewal. While “Reformations East and West”—a 1911 short essay by historian Hara Katsurō (1871–1924) that systematically compared German Protestantism and Japanese Buddhism—is often cited as the foundational work in this discourse, earlier examples abound. Although sixteenth-century European missionaries had noted similarities between Martin Luther’s movement and certain local religious groups, by the mid-nineteenth century, it was …

title: ‘Quoth the Raven’ — On Thought, Memory, Cognition, and Multispecies Engagements in Scandinavian Iron Age Beliefs and Society
abstract: Two non-humans from Old Norse mythology have achieved a popularity that eclipses some of the deities in the pantheon: corvids Huginn and Muninn. In pre-Christian Iron Age beliefs, Huginn and Muninn were the shrewd ravens of Óðinn, Allfather, the supreme god of the Æsir, the gods of the Old Norse tradition. These two ravens perched on Óðinn’s shoulders, and their names indicate that they represented thought (Huginn) and memory (Muninn). They were seemingly perceived as guardians of esoteric knowledge and magic in the Iron Age, and from their elevated position on the shoulders of the mightiest …

title: Planned behaviour during university-to-work transitions: lived implications for Japan’s Support Project for creating social impact through the internationalisation of universities
abstract: Drawing on the Theory of Planned Behaviour and employing Interpretive Phenomenological Analysis, this study investigates how nine Japanese students at a Top Global University Project-affiliated college interpret and navigate educational-vocational transitions amid the nation’s ongoing internationalisation reforms. More specifically, by centring their lived experiences, we aim to generate recommendations for Japan’s Support Project for Creating Social Impact through the Internationalisation of Universities that better align with the realities and aspirations of globally minded learners. …

title: A Critical Collection History of Nineteenth-century Women’s Letters: Overcoming the Occluded Archive with Data-Driven Methods
abstract: This paper presents a virtual archive of women’s epistolary exchange in 19th-century Finland. By harmonising metadata from over 1.2 million letters and over 100,000 correspondents across key cultural heritage organisations and leveraging linked open data, we gain an unprecedented view of 19th-century epistolary communication and 20th-century archival practices. Using quantitative analysis, enriched metadata, and network visualisations, we explore the gendered nature of these collections. Are women archival protagonists, or are their materials embedded within the collections of male relatives? …

title: Evaluating and Understanding the Geocoding of City Directories of Paris (1787-1914): Data-Driven Geography of Urban Sprawl and Densification
abstract: As in other western cities, the fast-paced urban, industrial, and commercial sprawl of Paris during the 19th century provided the backdrop and driving force for the publishing phenomenon of trade directories. We show how these collections of millions of nominative entries associated with addresses can be turned into a serial dataset whose massive, fine-grained, and geolocated nature opens up new possibilities for quantitative and multi-scale analyses of the dynamics at play during one of the most dramatic socio-spatial transformations of the city. We highlight the methodological conditions of …

title: Making Sense of the Emergence of Manslaughter in British Criminal Justice
abstract: Manslaughter emerged as a new and distinct category of crime amongst those tried at the Old Bailey in London in the first half of the nineteenth century. From being a rare charge in 1800, manslaughter came to represent over 60% of all trials for ‘killing’ by the 1850s. This article describes the methodologies used by the authors to explore this phenomenon via trials included in the Old Bailey Online. It details the use of unsupervised clustering, embeddings and relevance measures to map the changing language associated with the charge of manslaughter; and more importantly, describes the …

title: Assemblies of Points: Strategies to Art-historical Human Pose Estimation and Retrieval
abstract: This paper attempts to construct a virtual space of possibilities for the historical embedding of the human figure, and its posture, in the visual arts by proposing a view-invariant approach to Human Pose Retrieval (HPR) that resolves the ambiguity of projecting three-dimensional postures onto their two-dimensional counterparts. In addition, we present a refined approach for classifying human postures using a support set of 110 art-historical reference postures. The method’s effectiveness on art-historical images was validated through a two-stage approach of broad-scale filtering preceded by …

title: Image Reuse in Eighteenth-Century Book History: Large-Scale Data-Driven Study of Headpiece Ornament Variants
abstract: This study uses large-scale computational analysis to trace the reuse of decorative headpieces in eighteenth-century books. The results highlight how image variants reveal complex networks of printers and publishers beyond simple one-to-one ownership.

title: Introduction: History and Data Science: Data-driven Inquiries into the Past
abstract: The integration of data science methods into historical research is an emerging joint focus of digital humanities and history. This new research area applies data science methods to study large historical datasets, such as correspondences, chronicles, oral history interviews, photos, and maps. As part of the overarching goal to further our knowledge of the past, the application of data science methods in historical research involves an array of epistemological questions as well. For instance, what can count as evidence and knowledge in the context of data driven inquiries into the past?

title: Advocating for inclusive narratives: A call for critical engagement with the palm oil agribusiness sector
abstract: The palm oil industry, a significant economic driver in South-east Asia, remains at the centre of intense global scrutiny due to environmental and human rights concerns persist. Despite its high productivity per hectare, critics continue to raise concerns about its role in deforestation, biodiversity loss and exploitative labour practices. The industry’s transnational nature further complicates these debates, shaping public perception and policy discourse. Overwhelmingly, the narrative about this sector focuses on negative consequences, warning consumers of importing deforestation and …

title: The king’s word: Colonial contracting and financial capitalism in Moskitia during the scramble for Central America, 1824–42
abstract: Abstract This article examines how Miskitu King Robert Charles Frederic (1824–42) used colonial contracts with foreign merchants to advance his political agenda in Moskitia, on Central America’s Caribbean coast. Drawing on European and Central American archives, this study challenges narratives that portray Indigenous leaders as passive actors in colonial expansion, highlighting how the king strategically wielded contracts to facilitate the import of foreign capital through concessions and loans. His mastery of international finance enabled resistance to imperial domination while allowing him …

title: Cod and its oil, cuisine and its supplements: Fish fragmentation, commodity connections and naturalising resources in Newfoundland
abstract: By spotlighting cod liver oil as an example of a global fat and reflecting on the commercialisation of fish – from food source and medicine to dietary supplement – this article surveys cod’s colonial history in Newfoundland alongside cultural imaginations of resources. The oil’s popularity boomed in the early twentieth century with the discovery of vitamins, which gifted foods and their by-products new values. This article thus sketches out how fish, fat and commercial markets connect the history of cod liver oil in Newfoundland with the world. Prioritising three cultural artefacts – a folk …

title: Autarkic, but global: Fat supply and whaling in pre-war Nazi Germany
abstract: Nazi Germany started whaling in the Antarctic Ocean in 1936 as a result of its high dependence on fat imports and a shortage of foreign currency. While this was part of a policy geared towards self-sufficiency or autarky, whaling did not cut Germany off from the international links that characterise the global fat supply, but actually created new connections. The article sets out four new arguments. First, Germany never achieved self-sufficiency in whale oil or fat in general. Second, in the context of whaling, links to Norway remained strong. Third, the Anglo-Dutch Unilever group was a key …

title: Food chemistry, fat experiment and palm oil in late Soviet politics and industry
abstract: This article discusses the development of food chemistry in the Soviet Union beginning in the late 1950s. It analyses how, amid a growing cult of chemistry, scientists sought to address food crises and envisioned the creation of modern, scientifically engineered food. This study examines the scientific beliefs and experiments as well as their political relevance in response to persistent food shortage. Emphasising the fact that these experiments were successful in the laboratories but limited in industrial production, the article examines initiatives such as synthesising food – the project …

title: Whaling as an interim oil supply industry: The rise and fall of whale oil in the competitive fat and oil markets
abstract: Whale oil, a general term for products derived from the fats and oils of numerous cetacean species, is a global resource whose purveyors have historically been buffeted by economic, technological, and environmental forces. It remained a viable international commodity in the first half of the twentieth century due to a remarkable shift from its use mainly for lighting and lubrication to one used for food products such as margarine and even explosives, before it quickly faded as alternatives emerged and environmental regulations took hold. While previous studies have illuminated various aspects …

title: Fat: Lubricant of modernity
abstract: This article explores the global history of fat as both a vital nutrient and a versatile industrial commodity from the nineteenth to early twentieth centuries. The study highlights fat’s expanding applications – from foodstuffs like margarine and shortening to non-food products including soaps, paints and early plastics. Drawing on historical data and trade patterns, it reveals how colonial and geopolitical dynamics shaped resource preferences. The article calls for situating fat within broader narratives of industrialisation, globalisation, and imperialism and integrating it into commodity …

title: Global entanglements of palm oil and kernel extraction from French West Africa (c. 1840–1960)
abstract: This article links the regional history of palm oil and kernel extraction in French West Africa to the global history of fat resources. It argues that what happened to fat resources produced and consumed elsewhere is crucial to understanding how the extraction of West African palm products developed over time. The article illustrates how the French became interested in West African palm oil in the nineteenth century in their search for fats for soap production, and how the colonial conquest of the region was linked to the West African groundnut crisis. In the twentieth century, the way in …

title: Fish oil’s journey through Russian and Soviet history
abstract: Throughout Russian, Soviet and post-Soviet eras, fish oil has repeatedly changed its role as scientific and technological advances rendered earlier uses obsolete. Originally prized by coastal communities as a dense caloric supplement, it evolved into a cornerstone source of vitamins A and D and later achieved prominence through its rich omega-3 profile, after these fatty acids were recognised for health. In Soviet times, fish oil transcended its nutritional and medicinal roles to become a tool of state health policy and a miraculous lifeline, in particular during the Siege of Leningrad. …

title: Roots and dynamics of Dutch foreign plant-oil demands 1920–2020
abstract: Dutch harbours became key notes in European foreign fat supply in the twentieth century. These imports of oils and fats have had significant economic, social and environmental impacts worldwide. Demand for these resources was driven by food industries, intensive livestock farming and fossil fuel mitigation, and linked domestic practices to global supply chains. This paper investigates the development of Dutch imports of oils and fats over the past century. It examines (1) the scale and geographical distribution of these resources, analysing growth, decline and spatial shifts in supply; and …

title: O “LIVRO DIDÁTICO E MANUAIS DE HISTÓRIA” COMO CATEGORIA DE PESQUISA EM HISTÓRIA E EDUCAÇÃO STRICTO SENSU NO BRASIL (1991-2017): O ESTADO DO CONHECIMENTO
abstract: This text presents the results of a study on history textbooks and manuals in Brazil, based on a methodological approach aimed at locating, retrieving, compiling, selecting, and organizing references on History and its teaching available in the digital repository of theses and dissertations of the Coordination for the Improvement of Higher Education Personnel (CAPES). A total of 660 studies were identified in Graduate Programs in History and Education from different Brazilian universities, which were mapped into seven categories. This paper focuses on analyzing the production of one of these …

title: Global Maoist optics among diaspora: The Indian Workers’ Association during India’s food ‘crisis’, 1965–69
abstract: Abstract This article considers the responses of the Indian Workers’ Association (Great Britain) (IWA) to food scarcities in India during the late 1960s. It reveals Maoist optics informed IWA critiques, departing from coexistent appraisals articulated in leftist circles in India. In doing so, the article demonstrates the relevance of worldviews, idioms, and paradigms emanating from global conjunctures beyond places of origin among diaspora. IWA luminaries were embedded in revolutionary anti-colonial networks shaped by decolonization and the global Cold War, and bestowed substance upon Maoism …

title: Rethinking global Catholicism from Ottoman Europe: Catholic missions and local agency in the early modern world
abstract: Abstract This article investigates the role of Catholic and non-Catholic local actors in shaping missionary activities in seventeenth-century Ottoman Europe. It examines jurisdictional conflicts and collaborations between Bosnian Franciscan friars, Ragusan merchants, Ottoman officials—particularly judges—and Serbian Orthodox clergy, whose interactions shaped the local landscape of Catholicism and defined the limits of Catholic engagement. Drawing primarily on Catholic missionary sources, the study argues that analysing missions through interconnected local, regional, and global lenses, while …

title: Globalizing the international refugee regime: UNHCR’s expansion to Lebanon in 1962
abstract: Abstract The global expansion of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) is an understudied area of research, particularly in the Middle East. The issue is often framed through a linear, state-centric lens that oversimplifies its complexities and subordinates the role of microprocesses and individual actors. This article contributes to global and refugee history through a microhistorical study of the establishment of UNHCR’s branch office for the Middle East in Beirut in 1962. It challenges the assumption that UNHCR’s globalization process unfolded in a systematic and …

title: Digital heritage and fashion: preserving cultural identity through AI and virtual archives
abstract: Abstract The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) image generation presents both opportunities and challenges for preserving fashion heritage and cultural identity. This study aims to evaluate AI’s capacity to replicate historical fashion by introducing the Multi-Dimensional Fidelity Assessment (MDFA) framework, which combines computational perceptual similarity (LPIPS) with expert-scored cultural feature concordance (CFC). Applying MDFA to 15 ensembles generated by Gemini and ChatGPT, findings reveal a divergence between automated metrics and human judgment. While AI often achieves …

title: Animism meets posthumanism: reimagining the human–nature relationship through shrine gates ( torii ) in the works of Miyazaki Hayao and Shinkai Makoto
abstract: How can we rethink the human-nature relationship in the Anthropocene? Posthumanist approaches offer a critique of anthropocentrism, but often implicitly appropriate spiritual approaches, and explicitly dismiss one of these - animism - as premodern, negating the theoretical possibility of exploring the human-nature relationship charged with animistic imagination. We argue that films by Miyazaki Hayao and Shinkai Makoto can work as a medium to transcend these limits of posthumanism and offer a pathway for understanding humans’ connection with nature. Specifically, the imagery of the shrine …

title: Teaching the history of the ‘fifteen years’ war’ in Japanese junior high schools: teachers’ aims, approaches, and strategies
abstract: Controversy has long surrounded the treatment of the 1931–1945 period in Japan’s history education. However, studies to date have largely focused on history textbooks. This study scrutinises how controversial topics were dealt with in junior high school classrooms, through interviews with 21 teachers in three areas of Japan, alongside lesson observations where possible. It was found that teachers usually taught about some controversial topics, but not necessarily at length. Influences upon the teaching of such topics included educational structures, past-related scholarship, social and …

title: REALISM OR IDEALISM? PERSPECTIVES ON THE PHILOSOPHY OF HISTORY FROM A PRACTICING HISTORIAN
abstract: ABSTRACT This review essay argues that the realist philosophy of history, as represented by Adam Timmins in Towards a Realist Philosophy of History , raises interesting questions about the nature of historical writing and challenges some of the foundations of idealist philosophy of history. A basic problem with Timmins's book is the conflation of “constructivism” with “idealism” when there are, indeed, quite a few “realists” who are also “constructivists.” After summarizing the main arguments of the book and critically examining them, this essay argues that realism, if combined with …

title: ON HISTORICAL (ANTI‐)REALISM
abstract: ABSTRACT The problem of historical realism has gained some new momentum recently, with a fresh challenge to what is taken to be an anti‐realist hegemony in the theory and philosophy of history. Unfortunately, this has also provided the opportunity for the reheating of old polemics and lazy scholarship that characterized the 1990s reaction to “postmodernism.” Ill‐defined questions distract us from more important issues. Here, I offer a map that aims to clarify the conceptual space. I distinguish between a metaphysical problem, which is the problem of historical realism proper, and an …

title: UNIVERSALITY IN THE CLIMATE CATASTROPHE: RETHINKING CHAKRABARTY'S ANTHROPOCENE PHILOSOPHY OF HISTORY WITH MERLEAU‐PONTY'S PHILOSOPHY OF NATURE
abstract: ABSTRACT This article critically examines Dipesh Chakrabarty's concept of Anthropocene history, a philosophy of history that is designed to respond to the universal challenge of the Anthropocene. It uses the work of Maurice Merleau‐Ponty to mitigate the pitfalls of Chakrabarty's concept and to propose an alternative relation between nature and history. I argue that the problem of Chakrabarty's Anthropocene history resides not in its use of the category of the universal per se but in its insufficient articulation of the particular. Even if he is correct in asserting that it is impossible to …

title: ‘But Their Mouths are Sealed’: Medical Practitioners in French Colonial Courtrooms, 1828–1848
abstract: Abstract This article sheds light on a previously overlooked aspect of medical practice in colonial contexts: the involvement of medical practitioners in legal proceedings. It emphasizes that medical expertise was not solely utilized for diagnosing and treating patients in the disease-ridden environment of the Caribbean colonies, but also for explaining sudden and/or violent deaths. From the late 1820s onwards, driven by the abolitionist movement and legal reforms, there was a notable surge in trials where enslavers faced accusations of mistreating and killing enslaved individuals. This …

title: Research on graph-retrieval augmented generation based on historical text knowledge graphs
abstract: Abstract This article addresses domain knowledge gaps in general large language models for historical text analysis in the context of computational humanities and AIGC technology. We propose the GraphRAG framework, combining chain-of-thought prompting, self-instruction generation, and process supervision to create a “The First Four Histories” character relationship dataset with minimal manual annotation. This dataset supports automated historical knowledge extraction, reducing labor costs. In the graph-augmented generation phase, we introduce a collaborative mechanism between knowledge graphs …

title: Grassroots Officials, Worker Wrongdoings, and Masculinity in the Nantong Municipal Steel Rolling Mill, c. 1970
abstract: Abstract This article examines how competing ideals of masculinity were negotiated in the everyday life of a steel mill community in the People’s Republic of China during the early 1970s. Using the personnel dossier of a male worker from the Nantong Municipal Steel Rolling Mill, contextualized within a framework of archival sources, operational manuals, industry periodicals, textbooks, and newspapers, it explores how workshop culture, homosocial interactions, and heterosexual relationships shaped gendered norms. Within the mill, the state promoted an ideal of disciplined, self-controlled …

title: Race, Medicine, and Causation in the Eighteenth-Century Atlantic World
abstract: Abstract In December 1753, the South Carolinian physician, John Lining, wrote a letter to Dr Robert Whytt, Professor of Medicine at the University of Edinburgh, offering ‘A Description of the American Yellow fever’. ‘[T]his dreadful malady, which so frequently rages like the plague in the southern parts of America’, Lining observed, seemed to strike almost everyone: ‘both sexes of the white colour, especially strangers lately arrived from cold climates, Indian, Mistees, Mulattoes of all ages, excepting young children and of those only such as had formerly escaped the infection’. Peculiarly, …

title: History textbooks and political power in contemporary Japan: controversial representations, pedagogy, and national identity
abstract: Abstract Contention about representations of history and the purposes of History education has long surrounded Japanese History textbooks. From 2012, the ascent of powerful nationalist Prime Minister Abe Shinzō raised questions about possible political pressures on textbook content. This article analyzes recent market-leading junior high school and high school History textbooks to discover how pedagogical format and content related to controversial topics or national identity have changed since 2012. It finds that leading junior high school textbooks have largely maintained their …

title: Minor transnational engagements in the making of the Japanese recording industry
abstract: Abstract This article explores the early development of Japan’s recording industry, focusing on locally driven “minor transnational engagements” between emerging Japanese record companies and foreign recording experts. The initial phase of Japan’s recording history mirrored the pattern in most countries from the early 1900s, with major record companies organizing international recording expeditions equipped with new acoustic disc recording technology. However, it was homegrown firms in the 1910s, especially the Nipponophone Company (Nihon Chikuonki Shōkai 日本蓄音器商會), that positioned themselves …

title: Aetiological Politics, Mental Illness, and Affective Neuroscience in British Slave Trade Abolition
abstract: Abstract The role of medical science, including testimony from medical practitioners during Britain’s parliamentary inquiry into the slave trade, has eluded sustained scrutiny in the historiography. Through a close reading of parliamentary hearings, doctors’ clinical reasoning, diagnostic practices, and therapeutic protocols emerge as key forensic evidence in the abolition movement. This article traces the politics of medical diagnosis by studying mental illnesses such as melancholia, hysteria, and insanity on British slave ships and as they were debated in parliament. Building upon the …

title: The ambivalent utopia: layers of nostalgia and memory in Murakami Haruki’s The City and Its Uncertain Walls
abstract: Scholarship has often been skeptical about nostalgia in Murakami’s narratives of self-discovery in postwar and late-capitalist Japan. This article, however, takes a different view, suggesting that nostalgia has a constructive role. This article explores the tension between two layers of nostalgia—the individual and the instrumental—in Murakami’s latest publication, The City and Its Uncertain Walls. In this novel, nostalgia helps the narrator reconstruct his self-identity and continuity by critically re-engaging with his past, transforming it into a meaningful personal narrative. However, it …

title: An Advertisement Ahead of Its Time?
abstract: The 2022 US Supreme Court decision in Dobbs v. Jackson was met with dismay among supporters of reproductive rights and justice, both in the US and globally. For some commentators on India, it was also occasion for pride in Indian abortion law. In the months before the Dobbs decision was announced, the Indian legislation that governs abortion, the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act of 1971, had been amended to allow abortion until twenty weeks of gestation, and until twenty-four weeks and beyond in certain circumstances. Among social media posts that highlighted this divergence between …

title: Forging Sea Power: Pacific Naval Developments 1865–1900
abstract: This important new study offers a fresh perspective on the emergence of the “new” US Navy in the 1890s; one shaped by a dynamic period of naval development on the west coast of South America, and across the Pacific, where Chile, Peru, China, and Japan developed impressive modern fleets from European models. Jamison uses the concept of transwar to link a succession of maritime conflicts that stretched from Cape Horn to Chingdao to the US Civil War, and the wider engagement of European shipbuilding, armaments, and technologies. abstract: The now-archaic botanical term "cryptogam" was used to refer to ferns, mushrooms, and other plants thought to reproduce without producing seeds. In Japanese, however, the term cryptogam (inka shokubutsu) has been used as a metaphor for queer sexualities since shortly after World War II. Starting in the early 1950s, inka shokubutsu began to be used to refer to queer communities emerging in Tokyo and other urban centers and was subsequently adopted by mainstream media during the 1960s and 1970s. title: Withdrawal and Belonging: Ethnographic Insights from a Hikikomori Rehabilitation Center in Japan
abstract: Abstract This research note examines how people labeled as hikikomori —prolonged social withdrawal—navigate isolation, moral judgment, and attempts at rehabilitation. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork in a rural rehabilitation center, it situates their experiences within broader social transformations in post-industrial Japan. Departing from accounts that frame hikikomori primarily through diagnosis or individual pathology, this note foregrounds lived experience and the moral dimensions of rehabilitation. abstract: Abstract This article examines how Berlin’s Statue of Peace, created through transnational feminist civil society, became entangled with South Korean Minjung nationalism during the 2024 removal controversy. title: Parental Rights to Religious Education in Contemporary Japan: A Comparative Law Perspective
abstract: Abstract This article re-examines parental rights to religious education in contemporary Japan in light of post-2022 debates over “religious abuse” and shūkyō nisei , or people raised in religious families. title: Photographs as Action: The All-Japan Students’ Photo Association and the Making of Eco-Critical Photography in Japan, 1960s–2020s
abstract: Abstract This article examines the All-Japan Students’ Photo Association’s (AJSPA) 1970 “Pollution campaign” as a pivotal intervention in photographic practice and public activism. title: The Cultural Catch: Japanese Whaling Fiction and the Gender(ed) Politics of Nostalgia
abstract: Abstract This article reads the post-moratorium boom in historical whaling fiction against shifting debates over the legitimacy of Japanese whaling. Taking Itō Jun’s Kyogei no umi (2013) as example, I draw on critical heritage studies and Svetlana Boym’s theory of nostalgia to show how the novel reconstructs Edo-period whaling as a morally coherent, patriarchal community built on self-sacrifice and masculine heroism. title: Storm of Progress: The Politics and Literature Debate and the Art of Nakamura Hiroshi
abstract: Abstract This paper discusses the work of Japanese painter Nakamura Hiroshi in the late 1950s and early 1960s in light of the politics and literature debate raging among the Japanese intelligentsia in the immediate post-World War II era, focusing specifically on the exchange between Kurahara Korehito and the writers associated with the Kindai bungaku literary journal. title: Using the News to Measure International Cooperation: Evaluating Japan–ROK Government Cooperation Using the GDELT 2.0 Event Database
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how well news articles reflect levels of interstate cooperation, focusing on cooperation between the Japanese and the South Korean governments. title: “Japan as Savior, Japan as Invader”: Indonesian Youth Perceptions of Japan in the Pacific Wartime
abstract: Abstract Students’ understanding of Japan’s arrival in Indonesia during the Pacific Wartime (1942–45) sparks a sharp conflict in narratives: was Japan a savior or an invader? title: Negotiating the (Im)Possibility of Contested Memory: The Traveling “Comfort Women” Memorial in Kyoto, Japan
abstract: Abstract Since its first installation in December 2011 in front of the Japanese Embassy in Seoul, South Korea, the P’yŏnghwaŭi Sonyŏsang —widely known as the Statue of a Girl for Peace or “Comfort Women” Statue—has been replicated and installed around the world. title: Forgetting and Remembering: The Conflict Over the Collective Memory of the Filipina “Comfort Women” of the Asia-Pacific War
abstract: Abstract This article examines the forgetting of the collective memory of the Filipina “comfort women” prior to the 1990s transnational redress movement. It argues that the prevailing social norms around prostitution, postwar narratives of heroism versus collaboration, and the interests of state and elite actors contributed to the initial silencing of this memory. title: Expo 2025 Overexposure: Tracing Mega-Event Media Narratives and Official Discourses of the Expo and the Olympics in Japan
abstract: Abstract How was the Expo 2025 in Osaka spun and marketed to the public vis-à-vis the news media discourse? title: “Here was Manila”: Visualizing the 1945 Battle of Manila on YouTube
abstract: Abstract The 1945 Battle of Manila, one of the Asia-Pacific War’s deadliest urban battles, remains marginalized in scholarly and commemorative memory even as it circulates widely online. This article examines how YouTube videos represent the battle through spatial narratives: military operations, architectural destruction, and marginalized civilian experiences. By analyzing 17 videos, the article interrogates how content creators transform urban catastrophe into abstract space, shaped by archival constraints and YouTube’s platform affordances. title: The Korabo -Rationality of Time in Bungo Stray Dogs
abstract: Abstract Recently, a form of media production known as korabo has become vital to success in Japan’s popular media industries. Korabo ’s swift systematization stems from its integration into the media mix production system that already dominated Japan’s media environment. Through a close analysis of the Bungo Stray Dogs media mix franchise and its evolution over time, this article examines the effects of the korabo system on the physical environment of an Earth threatened by manmade climate change. title: The Uncomfortable Memory of the Spanish Community in the Philippines
abstract: Abstract The Spanish community in the Philippines was able to define its own collective memory for decades during the first decades of the 20th century, much like in Latin American counterparts. However, from the beginning of the Commonwealth (1935), the long transitional period to the end of the colonial period, its capacity to transmit and define its collective memory crumbled, triggered by external events. title: Disinformation and Conspiracy Narratives in the Online Media Strategy of Happy Science (Kōfuku no Kagaku)
abstract: Abstract This article examines the online media strategy of the religious group “Kōfuku no Kagaku” (Happy Science) and its political arm “Kōfuku Jitsugentō” (Happiness Realization Party) through two analyses: a quantitative analysis of the group’s news outlets and a qualitative analysis of a YouTube channel. title: The US Merchant Marine Academy and Students from the Philippines: Memory and Historical Narrative in the Postwar Era
abstract: Abstract The United States government sought to rehabilitate the devastated Philippines through a scholarship for Filipino youths at the United States Merchant Marine Academy. Many Filipinos fought against the Japanese bravely and endured much hardship during the war on the side of the United States, including a significant portion of the cadets sent to the academy. Their stories were captured in a cadet corps magazine called Polaris , in which they described their experiences of war in gruesome detail, but in a way clearly influenced by the liberation narratives of the Japanese imperialists.

title: Travel in Japan’s Postgrowth Hyperrealities and National Conservative Ideology: Shinkai Makoto’s Suzume No Tojimari
abstract: Abstract Suzume no tojimari (2022) depicts the coming-of-age road trip of a teenage girl through abandoned places, in order to save Japan from giant earthquake worms, and to confront her own past of 3/11. title: Tōjō Hideki, Storytelling, and the Emotional Politics of Hope in Wartime Japan
abstract: Abstract Imperial Army General and wartime Prime Minister Tōjō Hideki is widely reviled today as a dictator or a war criminal. But in the early years of his premiership (1941–1944), he was a media darling, praised as a decisive leader and a warmhearted human being. This article spotlights wartime storytelling about Tōjō’s past and family life. It shows how media used biographical stories to champion an emotional politics of hope and unite the public behind Japan’s wartime leadership. title: Nothing New? Bureaucratic Reforms and the Reorganization of the Ministry of Communications (Teishinshō) in Occupied Japan (1945–1952)
abstract: Abstract This article reconsiders prevailing assumptions of bureaucratic continuity in postwar Japan by examining the case of the Ministry of Communications during the Allied Occupation. abstract: This paper presents the stories of three Asian elephants — Arikomban, Kalloor Komban, and Soorya—who live in a landscape of conflict, coexistence, survival, and captivity in the Western Ghats of South India. abstract: Placing the special issue within the historiography of human-elephant relationships, the introduction addresses the challenges associated with the integration of elephants into academic narratives. abstract: This article explores the biography of Geeltje’s Adema, a prominent breeding bull in post-war Polish agricultural discourse, to examine the ideological dimensions of animal biographies within the context of human-animal relations and agricultural modernization. abstract: This article examines the invention and exhibitions of the panda circus to explore the political, economic, and cultural influence of the giant panda on China–Japan diplomacy and the transnational cultural economy. abstract: This article examines the relationship between photographic practice, visual epistemologies and iconographies of crisis, and the racialized and economically regulated infrastructures of COVID-19 in the Global South—including infrastructural transformations of built and non-human environments. title: Public art as Public History: Stuart Brisley and 1970s Britain
abstract: This article investigates the nature of the ‘public’ in public history by returning to a crucible moment in 1970s Britain when public art and public history were not clearly differentiated. title: Upstream disciplinarity to move beyond it? The interdisciplinary scholarship of survivor scholars after the Holocaust
abstract: This article examines the methods of ‘early Holocaust research’ developed by Jewish survivor scholars after WWII and interprets them as profoundly innovative, integrating inherited scholarly gestures and memorial practices associated with the Jewish tradition, as well as ethnographic and historiographical methods developed during the interwar period. abstract: This article delves into the discipline of archaeology as well as the sub-discipline of digital and computational archaeology to explain various forms of interdisciplinary work within them. With the help of three case studies, this article shows different approaches to, and levels of, interdisciplinarity and how these enrich the interpretation of the past. title: Sewing machines, intercommunal violence, and the economic order of things in the late Ottoman empire
abstract: Abstract The global diffusion of sewing machines required concerted efforts from manufacturers, sales agents, and, most significantly, local consumers, who rendered the machine legible and desirable across diverse social settings. title: Ballast: Approaching nineteenth-century maritime mobility ‘from below’
abstract: Abstract This article explores the nineteenth-century history of ship’s ballast to study global maritime mobility ‘from below’, both socially and materially. Though mostly overlooked by contemporaries and historians alike, ballast was both a necessary resource for and a constraint on sea travel. This article examines ballast in four steps. First, it defines ballast in terms of its function, materiality, and value. title: Anthoine de Gogorza, Louis Lacharme, and the forgotten origins of the Panama Canal
abstract: Abstract The story of the Panama Canal is often framed as a morality tale juxtaposing French tragedy and American triumph (or imperialism). What gets lost in this depiction is a pair of adventurous entrepreneurs, Anthoine de Gogorza and Louis Lacharme, whose efforts led Ferdinand de Lesseps to his doomed canal project. This article shows how the roots of the Panama Canal emerged from the forests of Colombia’s Sinú River Valley, whose settlement, in turn, was fostered by the search for canal routes in the Darien. abstract: Abstract The exchange of raw cotton and consumer textiles has been widely portrayed as a core element of European imperialism in Africa. abstract: Abstract Between the 1890s and the 1940s, a diverse group of Chilean diplomats, businessmen, and intellectuals sought to convert Japan into a principal consumer of Chile’s struggling nitrate fertilizer industry (saltpetre). title: Ikigai or illusion? Precarity, relationality and estrangement in Sayaka Murata’s Convenience Store Woman
abstract: Sayaka Murata’s Convenience Store Woman offers a critique of the existential dispossession wrought by neoliberal precarity in late-capitalist Japan. title: Eurasian exchanges: Central Asian nomadic pastoralists, mountain ecosystems, and market economies in the early twentieth century
abstract: Abstract What role did nomadic and non-settled societies play in the early twentieth-century world economy? Exploring a remote mountain valley close to the border between the Russian and Qing empires, this article investigates the multiscalar history of the Karkara trade fair and its Kazakh and Kyrgyz pastoralist communities. title: Rising Seas, Sinking Lands: Reckoning with Local and Global Sea Level in the Early Modern Netherlands
abstract: This article examines notions of rising seas in the early modern Dutch Republic and explores how Dutch water management spurred efforts to think and act across scales. Focusing on a 1731 report by the surveyor Nicolaas Cruquius, it shows how environmental, political, and epistemological concerns shaped Dutch perceptions of rising seas. abstract: A common theme in the historiography related to Oda Nobunaga is his strong opposition to religious institutions. abstract: Abstract Chinese local product records in traditional gazetteers constitute a vital component of cultural heritage. abstract: Abstract The contemporary discourse surrounding the Japanese “Chinatown” relies on the “antinomy of Chinese humanity.” This antinomy holds together two individually reasonable statements: first, that a Chinatown houses Chinese inhabitants, and second, that no essential characteristic of Chinese people or Chinatowns exists. abstract: Abstract This article disentangles the complex web of social relations in and across Okinawa, Brazil, Japan, and the United States as represented in Medoruma Shun's 1999 short story “My Brazilian Granddad's Sake.” The story focuses on an elderly Okinawan man who develops a friendship with a young boy around the time of Okinawa's reversion to Japan in 1972 and passes down his memories of his migration to Brazil in the 1920s and his family's deaths during the Battle of Okinawa. title: Predicting the Past
abstract: Absences pervade the historical record. The loss or destruction of material, redaction of documents, silence of participants, data embargoes, and poor record keeping present inherent difficulties to any understanding of the past. Gaps in the historical record pose significant challenges but they can also provide valuable opportunities. Instead of avoiding all gaps, historians can test the accuracy of some inferences about the past by carefully outlining their assumptions and explicitly predicting what they believe to have occurred in the absence of evidence. abstract: This paper offers a philosophical appraisal of the role truth commissions might play in addressing the legacy of colonial injustice in contexts that do not fit the paradigmatic model of transitional justice. abstract: ABSTRACT This provocation calls readers to think more deeply about the role anthropology could play in radically disrupting plant blindness. abstract: Intersectional feminist work around digital archiving can productively develop stack models to address questions concerning the location, site, and materiality of possible and effective feminist intervention. abstract: In this article, I investigate the intersection between oral history, the possibility of the future, and post-anthropocentric approaches. abstract: In Enslaved Archives: Slavery, Law, and the Production of the Past, Maria R. abstract: Abstract As gateways into accessing the past, and catalogues of the cultures—and their biases—that we inherit, there are various research possibilities and limitations when considering library and museum online collections as sources of data. This study analyses different perspectives on how Jewish and Armenian ethnic minorities are represented by digital online collections of major historical museums. title: Oral history from an anti-colonial perspective: temporal and anthropocentric traps
abstract: This article explores the conceptual pitfalls of temporality and anthropocentrism from an anti-colonial perspective. Based on the narratives of Merina, a Kaiowa indigenous woman, the text discusses how ethnic memory, based on non-anthropocentric elements, challenges temporal linearity and colonial/modern and Eurocentric power structures. abstract: ABSTRACT A central question for European philology, informed by various agendas and ideologies, concerned comparison and the positing of hierarchies among languages. title: THE STAKES OF PHILOLOGY: REALITIES, ORIGINS, FUTURES
abstract: ABSTRACT What does philology mean today? And what can it do in the future? In this article, I respond to these questions by performing—again—a “return to philology,” as Paul de Man proclaimed in the 1980s. To engage with the present and future of philology, I return to nineteenth‐century Germany and to some of the controversies that played out between the main proponents of the new discipline, including Gottfried Hermann, August Boeckh, Friedrich Nietzsche, and Ulrich von Wilamowitz‐Moellendorf. title: TOWARD A CONJECTURAL HISTORY OF CONJECTURAL HISTORIES
abstract: ABSTRACT Most intellectual historians use the term “conjectural history” to designate a new form of speculative history created in eighteenth‐century Scotland by Adam Smith and a few others. These writers traced the development of human society and culture through conjectural reasoning based on philosophers’ views about human nature and travelers’ accounts of “primitive” peoples. title: Fragments, not prompts: five principles for writing history in the age of AI
abstract: This article offers five principles for historical writing in the age of generative AI — principles shaped not by fear of machines but by a confrontation with their fluency. As tools like ChatGPT increasingly saturate education, research, and public discourse, historians must reckon with what these systems can and cannot do. They summarize but do not listen, reproduce but do not interpret, and excel at coherence but falter at contradiction. This article explores some of them in relation to the tensions between two different but overlapping approaches to the history of concepts: philology and computationally informed historical semantics. abstract: Abstract As a form of art, literature is always concerned with human experience. title: Internationalism as lived experience: some critical reflections
abstract: The question of lived experience has been on the agenda of historians of internationalism for more than a decade. However, little effort has been made to engage with the new history of experiences literature. This experimental/conceptual article considers the potential that this literature holds for studying the history of internationalism. It does so by discussing three distinct but interconnected points: the importance of features of past perception, the need to reconsider the concept of agency and the notion of collective experience.

abstract: Research on host country human capital (HCHC) identified two kinds of effects it has on migrants: the facilitation of their integration into the host society and undocumented entry. This study seeks to reveal yet another effect of HCHC. Specifically, focusing on South and Southeast Asian students in Japan—the largest part-time laboring international student body in the country—it examines how their accumulation of HCHC may promote their semi-compliance (i.e., working in violation of employment restrictions while having legal residency). The analysis is primarily based on the results of …

title: Movers and haters: dynamic network visualization and analysis of an historical French controversy
abstract: Abstract This article presents the results of a novel, mixed-methods project that studied an eighteenth-century French debate about education reform using approaches from Social Network Analysis and contemporary Controversy Mapping, alongside traditional humanities methodologies. Toggling between close reading of over 200 texts, and distant reading of the whole debate as a network, revealed that this little-known polemic—which we call the Querelle des collèges—was one of many early modern quarrels, and that its central actors were not straightforwardly those one might have expected. title: Challenging the colonial legacies of the Humboldt Forum in Berlin: voices from “below”
abstract: This article focuses on the experiences and perspectives of non-state actors challenging the colonial legacies of the Humboldt Forum, Germany’s leading cultural project over the past decades. Departing from an empirical qualitative study, it gives insights into how experiences of dissonance with mainstream discourses on colonialism lead individuals to reconceptualize historical truth, into the resources through which activists build accountability from below, and into the changes that have taken place within the Humboldt Forum over the past years. title: PREAMBULAR HISTORY: THE VIEW OF THE PAST IN KEY HUMAN RIGHTS INSTRUMENTS
abstract: ABSTRACT This article claims that the preambles of foundational human rights instruments, taken together, articulate a consistent view of the past. This view is firmly rooted in historical processes, embedded in metaphysical truths, and enacted in service of the future. Part 1 assesses the strengths and weaknesses of the “preambular approach to history” and selects four instruments from a group of twenty‐two: the United Nations Charter, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the Genocide Convention, and the International Criminal Court Statute. title: Growing and pruning the archive: an agent-based model to build letter correspondence networks
abstract: Abstract The selection and availability bias concerning digital archives can be a problem for empirical studies. In the context of historical correspondence networks, we still have limited information about how missing data can affect and hinder the variables of our interest. Along these lines, we introduce an agent-based model to reconstruct historical communication using letters. We use this model to simulate the letter-sending process and its subsequent archival. title: Cross-temporal pedestrian mobility: walking-after Nietzsche in the Upper Engadine
abstract: The article introduces a method of practicing historically informed pedestrian mobilities called walking-after. The method involves engaging with past pedestrian mobilities by means of researcher’s own walking. In discussing this cross-temporal mobility, the article blends methodological insights with an account of the author’s walking-after Nietzsche in the Upper Engadine, foregrounding the affective plane of walking on which the past and the present meet. Methodologically anchored in new walking studies and the idea of molecular mobilities, the text argues for affect-oriented research into …

abstract: Abstract Colonialism in Africa was a textual encounter, with writing operating as an essential tool for colonial governance as well as a visual embodiment of Western “rationality” and civilization. Somalis, a predominantly oral people spread out across five colonial territories in the Horn of Africa, resisted Latin-based orthographies for their language because of these associations, while anticolonial nationalism following the Second World War brought the orthography question to the forefront as Somalis vigorously debated the written form Somali should take. abstract: Abstract Historical transmission chains (isnads) are fundamental to verifying authenticity in Hadith literature, yet narrator identity resolution is a persistent challenge due to onomastic ambiguity and complex naming conventions. While traditional methods lack scalability and modern language models overlook crucial network structures, this study bridges the gap by synergizing structural and semantic information. title: Text mining Nahdawi discourses: topic modeling Taha Hussein’s reformist legacy
abstract: Abstract This study re-examines the intellectual, cultural, and literary legacy of Taha Hussein (1889–1973), a pivotal reformist thinker of the Arab Nahda (renaissance or awakening). Integrating computational methods from the digital humanities, specifically topic modeling applied to a 42-work corpus, with traditional close textual analysis, the study uncovers the structural and thematic patterns underpinning Hussein’s discourse on identity, modernization, and cultural reform. The analysis foregrounds on his syncretic humanism, which weaves together Egypt’s Pharaonic, Arab-Islamic, …

title: Reimagining nihonga for the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere: a study of Taiwanese artist Chen Jin’s Fragrant Orchid (1942) within the visual culture of wartime Japan
abstract: Born in Taiwan during Japanese colonial rule, painter Chen Jin (1907–1998) spent most of her early career in Tokyo. She studied at the Women’s School of Fine Arts and actively participated in art associations in the metropole. In 1946, she returned to Taiwan and continued her career there. Today, although she is highly acclaimed as a master of modern Taiwanese art, she is largely absent from the history of Japanese modern art. This article investigates Chen’s career and artworks on display in Tokyo to shed new light on the transformation of imperial Japan’s art world and the multivalent …

title: Negotiating Gender and Ethnicity: Colonial Korean Women Studying Art in Imperial Japan
abstract: This study focuses on Korean women who studied art in Japan during the colonial period. In particular, it examines the constraints imposed on them by both Korean and Japanese societies, as well as the relationship between their studies and social class. To provide a more nuanced understanding of the experiences of these women, this article compares their cases to those of their Korean male and Japanese female counterparts. As a result, this study reveals first that there were gender differences in the nature and purpose of Koreans’ art study abroad. Specifically, the studies pursued by women …

title: Imperial Intersectionalities in Pre-1945 Japan: Art-Historical Interventions – Introduction
abstract: This article introduces a special issue that approaches the culture of imperial Japan (1920s–1940s) through an art-historical lens, centred on the intersectionalities of gender, ethnicity, class, and the dynamics between nation and empire. Regarding time frame, the contributions primarily focus on the years around 1940, but the 1920s also come into view as a period during which the professionalisation of Japanese women artists took shape. The introductory article begins with a brief retrospection on the rise of gender-critical art history in Japan since the mid-1990s and then highlights the …

title: Imperial Feminism in Japan: on the activities of the Women Artists Patriotic Service Corps during the Asia-Pacific War
abstract: This article draws on Imperial Feminism (teikoku no feminizumu), a concept employed by Japanese scholars of women’s history since the 1990s, and applies it to art history to provide a more nuanced understanding of how women artists asserted individual agency within the repressive contexts of imperialism and patriarchy. It analyses the activities of the Women Artists Patriotic Service Corps (Joryū bijutsuka hōkōtai), a collective of around fifty creators from a variety of genres, including yōga (lit. title: Making Plastics Count: Citizen Science Beach Cleanups and the Ocean Plastic Pollution Crisis (1980s–2020s)
abstract: In the 1980s, women in Oregon, Texas, and New Jersey organized the first “citizen beach cleanups,” directing volunteers to not simply clean up but collate data on the number and type of trash washing up on American shores. These efforts introduced the wider public to ocean plastic pollution, thereby instigating a “second plastic crisis,” powerfully countering neoliberal framings of environmental responsibility that blamed litter on individuals. title: Opening the black box of EEBO
abstract: Abstract Digital archives that cover extended historical periods can create a misleading impression of comprehensiveness while in truth providing access to only a part of what survives. While completeness may be a tall order, researchers at least require that digital archives be representative, that is, have the same distribution of items as whatever they are used as proxies for. If even this representativeness does not hold, any conclusions we draw from the archives may be biased. In this article, we analyse in depth an interlinked set of archives which are widely used but which have also …

title: Crossing boundaries through corpora: innovative corpus approaches within and beyond linguistics. S. Buschfeld, P. Ronan, T. Neumaier, A. Weilinghoff, & L. Westermayer (eds)
abstract: Driven by breakthroughs in computational capabilities and the expansion of data-intensive paradigms, corpus-based methodologies are experiencing both disciplinary diffusion and substantial innovation in research design and application. title: Folding, Gardening, Jointing, Swirling: On Non-(Uni)Linear Modes of Thinking Historicity and Practicing History
abstract: Abstract If the bridge between the dimensions of past, present, and future has become as uncertain as the very notion that history follows a linear trajectory, alternative ways of engaging with the past are gaining increasing significance. This essay explores how non-(uni)linear conceptions of time can offer a more nuanced understanding of historical and contemporary worlds. title: Catalanising the Costa Brava: Local interests, global tourism, and the nationalist power of authenticity in the late twentieth century
abstract: Abstract Since the 1950s, Catalonia has remained one of Europe’s most popular tourism destinations. Throughout this period, however, Catalonia’s presentation to the world has changed dramatically. In this article, I explore claims to authenticity in Catalan tourism attractions and promotion, which emerged as shrewd marketing language in the increasingly competitive tourism market of the 1980s and 1990s. title: Colonial world-making and global knowledges at the early modern Cape of Good Hope
abstract: Abstract As the Cape of Good Hope was integrated into early modern colonial world-making projects, it came to be regarded as ‘the western part of the East Indies’. The initial elaboration of this imaginary was contingent upon the contours of Dutch mobility in the Indian Ocean and material exigencies on the ground at the Cape. Early commanders sought to transform the colony’s environment, culture, and demographic constitution into a mirror of their productive East Indian colonies. title: A Fishy Tale of the Nuclear Power Plant Never Built in Estonia: An Envirotechnical History of Energy, Fish, Land and Water Resources Planning at Lake Võrtsjärv
abstract: One of the most mysterious stories in Estonian energy history revolves around the planning of a nuclear power plant (NPP) at Lake Võrtsjärv between 1967–1972. Despite the absence of planning documents in the energy archives and the impracticality of an NPP given Estonia’s abundant oil-shale energy production, the story, though sounding fishy, is well established in media and oral sources. title: Guerrilla Media
abstract: Abstract This article examines guerrilla interventions in early 1920s japanophone media by migrating Korean writers and Japanese allies contesting the language of imperial treachery. Following the 1919 Korean independence uprising, metropolitan Japanese-language print was moved by discussions about the threat of anticolonial terrorism from so-called futei Senjin (“treacherous Korean malcontents”). abstract: This article presents a pilot study at the intersection of history and computer science, focused on annotating “privacy” as a historical concept in runaway slave advertisements from the 18th and 19th centuries. We developed a semi-supervised natural language processing (NLP) framework for event extraction, combining limited expert-annotated data with larger unannotated corpora. title: Visualising Art on the Threshold in the Palazzo Medici, Florence
abstract: This paper explores the visual and kinaesthetic experience of traversing the domestic interior in fifteenth-century Florence, and the selective permeability of its physical and conceptual thresholds. The exploration is framed by an analysis of the composition and original architectural context of Filippo Lippi's c.1450 *Annunciation* painting (now in the National Gallery, London), which was probably installed above one of the doorways on the piano nobile of the Palazzo Medici. title: Private Birth, Public Authority: Topic Changes from the Sixteenth to the Eighteenth Century in German Midwifery Books
abstract: This article examines the benefits and pitfalls of using topic modeling to analyze discursive changes in sixteenth- and eighteenth-century German midwifery books. These periods were marked by transformations in the perspectives of midwives’ knowledge and practices, providing important insight into how midwifery was discussed as a field between private practice and public legitimization. By highlighting topic changes in controlled corpora of midwifery writings from the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries, the article provides an overview of elements historians must pay attention to for future …

title: A Digital Reconstruction of Privacy in the Royal Apartments? Network Theory and the 1585 court ordinance of Henri III of France
abstract: Although the early modern French royal court was known for its relative accessibility to the monarch and his spaces, this accessibility has often been misinterpreted as a limited or even nonexistent privacy. King Henri III (1551-1589), in particular, envisioned a monarchy heightened by distance and sought to regulate such distance through court ordinances. This article examines Henri III's 1585 court ordinance and applies network theory and access diagrams to reconstruct the spatiality of privacy within the French royal apartment. abstract: The paper explores Louis XIV’s iconographic preferences, arguing that the selection of paintings within his broader Cabinet des Tableaux collection, as well as their arrangement in the Appartement du Roi, reveal a significant aspect of the French king’s private life. The research treats the Sun king’s extensive painting collection —931 works identified from inventories dated between 1671 and 1715— as a homogeneous source, focusing primarily on the iconographic content rather than their artistic value. title: A Monarch in Motion: Mapping the King's Private Correspondence
abstract: This paper explores the mobility, correspondence, and architectural legacy of Christian IV of Denmark (1577–1648) through the application of digital humanities methodologies. Drawing on a corpus of 865 digitized and transcribed letters, we employ Named Entity Recognition, reconciliation with the World Historical Gazetteer, and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to map both the king’s itinerary and the spatial imaginary embedded in his writings. title: Integrating AI in historical research: a new method to analyzing national narratives
abstract: Abstract This paper presents a human-machine collaboration method to integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into historical research, specifically in the analysis of national narratives. Using President Ronald Reagan’s portrayal of America as a case study, the paper demonstrates how AI tools like natural language processing, BERTopic., and generative large language models, when guided by historians, can streamline the analysis of national narratives, significantly enhancing research efficiency. abstract: Despite recent legal reforms, the concept of sexual harassment remains unclear in Japan. The current legal framework only covers incidents in workplaces, leaving victims outside the work environment without adequate protection. Despite the rising public awareness, a significant gap persists in understanding how victims process and respond to their experiences of sexual harassment. abstract: This analytical article, based on sources and primary literature, discusses the traditions that led to the establishment of the field of Eastern and Southeastern European history at the Faculty of Arts of Masaryk University in Brno and in non-university research environments. title: Crossing Boundaries: Rethinking “Japanese Religion” in the Anthropocene
abstract: This article uses the fiftieth anniversary of the JJRS as an occasion to reexamine the field, consider challenges and opportunities, and offer suggestions for how to bring Japanese religious studies more in tune with developments in adjacent academic fields and wider societal concerns. I argue that scholars of Japanese religion must engage more with the most pressing issues of our time and that they can do so by applying insights from the environmental humanities to their studies. title: The Politics of Essence: Towards a History of the Public Study of Buddhism in 1880s Japan
abstract: This article examines the early institutionalization of Buddhist studies in Meiji Japan, focusing on the University of Tokyo’s establishment of Buddhism as an academic discipline between the late 1870s and the 1880s. abstract: This article examines how scholars of religion attempted to influence education policy after World War ii. Building on the clout they had gained during the Allied Occupation of Japan, some religious studies scholars capitalized on a series of moral panics to argue that their style of teaching religion could contribute to society, experimenting with terminology such as “religious knowledge education,” “religious sensitivity education,” or “religious culture education” as they did so. abstract: This article aims to overcome the longstanding dichotomy between religion and philology in scholarly discourse on kokugaku. Specifically, it argues that philology as it was practiced by the paradigmatic figure of the kokugaku movement, Motoori Norinaga, not only borrowed certain philological methods of analysis from the Shingon Buddhist cleric Keichū but also took for granted the esoteric Buddhist understanding of language that formed the context for the practice of those methods. title: Robot Dogs and the Paw Patrol
abstract: This paper explores the cultural politics of the police dog by tracing the role of dogs in the fabrication and reproduction of an anthropocentric social order in line with the imperatives of racial capitalism. These imperatives are based on sorting forms of life in accordance with their proximity to a normative white humanity as part of a project of meeting capitalism’s shifting valorization requirements. title: Becoming Pheasant
abstract: Pheasants have long been considered the most hunted bird species in the world. No other “hunting animal” has been bred, released, and shot for as long and as intensively as the pheasant. In the Netherlands, after centuries of actively shaping these birds and the landscapes in which they were hunted, the rearing and release of pheasants is now prohibited. title: An Introduction to Marco Reggio’s Activism and Research
abstract: This introduction situates Marco Reggio as a significant critical voice in the Italian animal liberation movement and provides context for the English translation of the first chapter of his 2022 book Cospirazione animale. abstract: According to Raymond and Lorna Coppinger, experts in canine behaviour, sheepdog trialling with Border Collies is mostly for fun. abstract: Abstract The archives of the London Corn Trade Association shed light on how open competitive commodity markets expanded during the First Global Era in spite of hard, non-cooperative geopolitics. title: ‘All of Tokyo is a black market’: Postwar black markets as spaces of representation
abstract: This article examines representations of the black markets (yami-ichi) in Japanese literature and other media in the immediate postwar era. As both material and figurative space, the black markets played a central role in the economic and cultural life of postwar Tokyo and other Japanese cities, marking both a visible, familiar space of everyday life and an inaccessible domain of illicit activity. abstract: Abstract Institutional records and reports, letters, and logbook entries are often the bread and butter of historical research, and the experience of extracting the depth and texture of these resources draws us back to the archive. abstract: Abstract The Caribbean, with its focus on cash crop production, played a major role in the rise of England’s Atlantic trading system and the making of modern capitalism. Yet, there remains poor understanding of the processes by which the early colonizers built the economic and social capabilities necessary to extract wealth from an alien environment, and a common assumption that they relied overwhelmingly on metropolitan skills and knowledge. title: The Muslim world as heterotopia: Global encounters in interwar Europe

abstract: Abstract This study quantitatively analysed the thematic structure and temporal transitions in Saikaku Ihara’s ukiyo-zōshi using latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA), dynamic topic modelling (DTM), and Word2Vec. title: Defeating the Ideal Chronicler: The Problem with the Thought Experiment
abstract: Abstract In this Letter to the Editor, I argue that Danto’s Ideal Chronicler thought experiment in philosophy of history conflates the properties of events with the relations between events. title: Out of the Rubble of the Second World War: Post-War Reconstruction in China
abstract: Abstract Abstract This article argues that the late 1940s in China should be studied through the lens of post-war reconstruction, rather than as a precursor to the Chinese Communist Revolution. I show how the legacy of the Cold War continues to influence historical scholarship on the failure of the Nationalist Government’s efforts in reconstruction, and how a comparative approach rewrites this narrative. Chinese cities suffered as much destruction as those in European countries, Japan, and the USSR, and China was not alone in facing a wave of criminality and poor governance in the post-war …

title: Horses, Doping, and the Relationalities of Care at the Royal Hong Kong Jockey Club, 1969–1971
abstract: Abstract This article explores the relationalities of care involving horses and humans in the context of horse-racing. By examining the horse doping cases in the Royal Hong Kong Jockey Club ( RHKJC ) from 1969 to 1971, a historical analysis demonstrates how caring for these relations requires infrastructures and relationalities of care. As a powerful institution that regulated gambling within postwar Hong Kong, the RHKJC became embroiled with allegations of horse doping. The cases involved more than 50 horses during the 1969/70 racing season, resulting in a fatality for one horse. This …

title: Drawing Barbed Wire: The Tule Lake Scrapbook of 1942
abstract: In December 1942, teachers and Japanese Americans at the Tule Lake Relocation Center created a scrapbook for Elmer Shirrell, the camp’s outgoing director. The scrapbook reveals Tule Lake teachers’ moralizing about the camp through their depictions of its natural and built environments. The scrapbook depended on nature to express the tensions felt by teachers and prisoners who lived according to pioneer narratives in a racialized prison. As a visual source, the scrapbook invites viewers into a moment of deliberation about the camp, its purpose, and its effects.
